planting.note: Container-grown shrubs can also be planted in spring once soil is workable.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in an open, sunny position for the heaviest fruit set. Because this species is largely self-sterile, grow at least two seedling-raised plants (not clonal copies of the same individual) nearby to ensure cross-pollination for its signature pendulous clusters of translucent red berries. Prune only lightly after flowering to remove dead or crossing wood, since the arching habit and berry display are best left largely undisturbed. Berries persist into winter if birds do not strip them first.

planting.note: Spring planting from containers is also acceptable in colder zones.

directions: Site in a sheltered spot with morning sun and afternoon shade, since the glossy, semi-evergreen foliage can scorch in harsh winter wind. Fragrant white flower panicles appear in early summer on the previous year's growth, so prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed rather than in late winter. Fruit ripens from red to black and is attractive to birds. Established plants tolerate light shade well, making this a useful structural evergreen for a woodland-edge shrub border.

Grow this large shrub where its grey-felted, buddleja-like leaves can be appreciated up close, since the foliage texture rather than flower color is the main ornamental draw. Creamy white flower clusters open in late spring followed by blue-black fruit, though fruiting is sparse compared to showier viburnum relatives. Tolerant of a range of soils as long as drainage is adequate, and benefits from an annual mulch to retain moisture around the shallow root zone.

planting.note: Fall planting is also fine in milder zones.

directions: Plant in a sheltered woodland setting protected from strong wind, since the thick bristly stems and large velvety leaves are easily damaged in exposed sites. Lacecap flowerheads of pink-purple fertile florets ringed by white sterile rays appear in mid to late summer on new wood. This species suckers gently to form a broad thicket over time, so give it room to spread or confine the root zone if a tidier footprint is preferred. Keep soil consistently moist and enriched with leaf mold.

Choose a sheltered, humus-rich site with dappled shade, replicating the woodland margins of its native range in central and southern China. Lance-shaped leaves have a distinctly bristly texture and felted undersides, and lacecap flowerheads in violet-blue to pink tones open in late summer, later than most garden hydrangeas. Mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat, and protect from late spring frosts which can damage emerging growth.

Give this vigorous climber a sturdy support such as a trellis or large shrub to scramble through, since it reaches considerable height in a single season once established. Solitary white four- to six-tepaled flowers appear over summer and are followed by fluffy, decorative seed heads that extend visual interest into autumn. Keep the root zone cool and shaded while allowing the top growth to climb into sun, following the classic clematis planting rule of 'cool roots, sunny head.'

This compact, fine-textured species suits a trough, low trellis, or scrambling over small shrubs rather than a large arbor. Finely divided, fern-like foliage sets it apart from larger-flowered garden clematis, and nodding pale yellow bell-shaped flowers open through summer, followed by fluffy seed heads. Native to the cold steppe regions of northern China and Mongolia, it tolerates harsher winters than many ornamental clematis and appreciates a well-drained site that avoids soggy winter conditions.
